posts.title: Your AI agent has been working for 40 minutes.
posts.author: Ankur Kathuria
posts.snippet:
Your AI agent has been working for 40 minutes.

It has read documents, rejected two approaches, made a design decision, and is halfway through a deliverable.

Then its context window fills up.

What should it carry into the next window?

That is the problem context compaction solves.

Compaction reduces the working context while preserving the information the agent needs to continue. The hard part is deciding what matters.

Imagine an agent writing a technical whitepaper. A useful compacted state might say:

→ Goal: Explain an on-prem AI architecture to enterprise architects  
→ Decision: Use a two-tier inference design  
→ Constraint: Avoid unsupported performance claims  
→ Evidence: Sources and measurements already checked  
→ Open issue: Validate the network assumptions  
→ Next step: Draft the deployment section  

A generic summary like “We discussed the architecture and made progress” is much shorter. It is also nearly useless to the next step.

This is why I think compaction should be treated as part of the agent harness, not just a way to save tokens.

The harness needs to preserve decisions, constraints, evidence, unresolved questions, and the exact point where work should resume. And when a detail needs to be exact, the agent should be able to return to the original source.

For long-running agents, continuity is an engineering problem.

If your agent had to resume tomorrow, what information would it need to do the next step correctly?

posts.snippet:
🏮 AI Agent + Crypto: davvero verso un mercato da 50 trilioni di dollari?
La cifra cattura l’attenzione.
Ma il punto più interessante, secondo me, è un altro.

Nel 2026 iniziamo a vedere qualcosa che nei cicli precedenti era molto meno evidente: applicazioni on-chain con utilizzo misurabile, fee reali e comportamenti finanziari che non vivono più soltanto nei whitepaper. 

Dentro questa trasformazione stanno convergendo più narrative:
→ social trading
→ stablecoin
→ RWA
→ AI Agent

IDC stima circa 1,15 miliardi di agenti AI attivi entro il 2029, capaci complessivamente di eseguire 217 miliardi di azioni al giorno.
Ma qui serve una distinzione importante: un’azione non equivale automaticamente a una transazione economica. 

La vera domanda è cosa succede quando un agente deve:
→ acquistare dati
→ pagare un’API
→ comprare compute
→ interagire economicamente con un altro software

È qui che blockchain e stablecoin iniziano ad avere senso come infrastruttura: sistemi disponibili 24/7, programmabili e adatti a micropagamenti e settlement tra macchine.
BlackRock ha descritto questa convergenza parlando di AI come “machine-native intelligence” e crypto come “machine-native money”. 

Poi c’è il passaggio successivo.
Tokenizzare fondi, Treasury o credito significa portare la finanza tradizionale on-chain.
Ma il salto più interessante potrebbe essere la nascita di mercati costruiti direttamente per software autonomi: agenti che incassano, acquistano compute, pagano altri agenti e accedono a servizi finanziari. 

Ed è qui che torno ai famosi $50T.

Per arrivarci non basta una nuova altseason.
Servirebbero:
→ agenti capaci di generare vera attività economica
→ una parte significativa di quei flussi su infrastrutture crypto
→ applicazioni capaci di trasformare utilizzo e fee in valore sostenibile
Per questo oggi i 50 trilioni restano una tesi, non un dato. 

La domanda che terrei sul radar è molto più semplice:
non quanti AI Agent esisteranno, ma quanti diventeranno attori economici e chi riuscirà a catturare il valore che muoveranno.
Nel carosello provo a separare hype, dati e condizioni necessarie per capire dove potrebbe nascere davvero questo mercato.

Dalle trenches, il segnale spesso arriva prima del nome della narrativa.

posts.title: Vielleicht erleben wir gerade den Anfang vom Ende einer reinen Klickökonomie im digitalen Marketing.
posts.author: Markus Kellermann
posts.snippet:
Vielleicht erleben wir gerade den Anfang vom Ende einer reinen Klickökonomie im digitalen Marketing.

Ich beschäftige mich aktuell sehr intensiv mit der Frage, wie Publisher künftig vergütet werden können, wenn ihre Inhalte Kaufentscheidungen beeinflussen, aber durch Zero Click und AI Search immer seltener ein klassischer Klick entsteht. 

Genau dazu arbeite ich gerade an einem Whitepaper und an meinem Vortrag „Beyond the Click: Wie Content, Publisher und AI Search die neue Customer Journey im Commerce verändern“.

Umso spannender finde ich eine aktuelle Entwicklung bei Google. In einem neuen Pilotprojekt testet Google direkte Zahlungen für Inhalte, die Antworten in Gemini, AI Overviews oder AI Mode wesentlich mitprägen. Entscheidend ist dabei nicht mehr, ob der Nutzer anschließend auf die Website des Publishers klickt, sondern ob dessen Content einen relevanten Beitrag zur generierten Antwort geleistet hat. 

Genau das finde ich bemerkenswert, weil damit erstmals sehr deutlich anerkannt wird, dass Content auch vor dem Klick einen wirtschaftlichen Wert erzeugen kann. 

Bisher funktioniert die Logik im Affiliate Marketing meist einfach: 
Ein Publisher erzeugt einen Klick, daraus entsteht ein Sale und dafür erhält er eine Provision. 

In einer AI Search Customer Journey kann aber etwas völlig anderes passieren. Ein Publisher testet beispielsweise zehn Produkte und liefert damit die Grundlage für eine KI Empfehlung. 

Der Nutzer liest nur die zusammengefasste Antwort und kauft direkt beim Händler. Der Publisher hat die Kaufentscheidung beeinflusst, taucht in der klassischen Attribution aber möglicherweise gar nicht mehr auf.

Google unterscheidet deshalb bereits zwischen unterschiedlichen Formen von Wertschöpfung. Content kann eine KI Antwort inhaltlich prägen, als Quelle zitiert werden oder später tatsächlich einen Referral und eine Conversion auslösen. 
Diese Ebenen können zusammenfallen, müssen es aber nicht. 

Noch ist das Modell alles andere als perfekt. Publisher sehen aktuell offenbar nur einen monatlichen Vergütungsbetrag, aber nicht, welche Inhalte wie häufig genutzt wurden oder nach welchen Kriterien Google den Wert berechnet.

Trotzdem halte ich diesen Schritt für sehr relevant. Denn wenn sich dieses Prinzip durchsetzt, reden wir künftig möglicherweise nicht mehr nur über CPC, CPO oder Last Click, sondern über neue Währungen für digitalen Einfluss: Contribution, Grounding, Citations oder tatsächlichen Impact auf eine Kaufentscheidung.

Ich stelle mir daher die Frage, wenn eine KI mit dem Wissen eines Publishers eine Kaufentscheidung beeinflusst, sollte dann künftig nicht genau dieser Beitrag vergütet werden und nicht erst der Klick danach?

When something breaks, it traces exactly where — producing tamper-evident proof you can defend to an auditor, a regulator, or a court.

Chapter 35

Gridlock in Tanzania: The Upcountry Bus Strike and the Regulatory Rift

Abstract

On September 29, 2026, Tanzania’s long-distance passenger transport sector was facing significant disruption as upcountry bus operators and drivers mounted industrial action in protest against a newly introduced penalty system.

 Visual evidence of large numbers of buses standing idle at transport depots captures the scale of the disruption and the extent to which the dispute has moved beyond an ordinary regulatory disagreement.

The confrontation exposes a deeper tension between regulatory enforcement and the economic realities of Tanzania’s road-transport industry. While regulatory authorities have a legitimate responsibility to enforce road-safety standards, operators and drivers have raised concerns about the financial consequences of increasingly stringent penalties and enforcement practices.

 Where regulatory obligations are perceived as economically unsustainable or insufficiently consultative, compliance can become a source of conflict rather than cooperation.

This investigation examines the immediate causes of the strike, the economic pressures confronting the long-distance bus industry, the widening regulatory divide, and the potential consequences for passenger mobility and commercial activity. 

It argues that the dispute should be understood not simply as an industrial action but as a test of Tanzania’s broader model of transport governance.

 A sustainable resolution will require credible dialogue, transparent enforcement, effective appeals mechanisms, and a regulatory framework capable of protecting public safety without undermining the economic viability of the sector.

posts.title: September is ending. But for compliance teams, the work doesn’t end with the calendar.
posts.author: Verifitech
posts.snippet:
September is ending. But for compliance teams, the work doesn’t end with the calendar.

Across global markets, compliance expectations continue to evolve — from employment and identity checks to criminal-record screening, data protection, right-to-work requirements, and sector-specific obligations.

What makes this challenging?

A process that works in one market may not work the same way in another.

A hiring team screening candidates across the USA, UK, UAE, India, Ireland, and Singapore can face different rules, documentation requirements, data-handling expectations, and verification practices in each jurisdiction.

And sometimes, the risk isn't an obvious compliance failure.

It is the small assumption:

“We’ve always done it this way.”

Imagine an HR team hiring across three countries. Their verification workflow is efficient, their turnaround is fast, and their internal process has worked for years.

Then one market introduces a new requirement.

Nothing in the workflow immediately breaks. Candidates still move through the process. Reports still arrive.

But the process is no longer aligned with the local requirement.

That is why compliance close-outs matter.

They give HR, compliance, and talent teams an opportunity to pause, review what changed, and ask:

Are our verification processes still fit for every market we operate in?

As September closes, it may be worth reviewing the regulatory and screening changes affecting your hiring markets — before they become operational problems.

You dumb. Grrr?!

We live in awful times. This could be the opening to any kind of topic, so let me narrow it down: we live in awful times, socially. The divide is stronger than ever, on wealth, on culture, on age, on pretty much everything. And on every topic the cards seem incredibly stacked against you. Even more so on the internet.

Take me, a 43 year old, college educated, cis, white, West German male, living “up the mountain”. I work remotely on my many start-ups and products, AI work no less, meaning I am self-employed. Right now my left eye is recovering from a two week stye, and the other one is tearing up in sympathy. I am practically looking for insults. And the internet is made for it.

With my recent endeavours in automating my life away, I tend to post more randomly across all channels. And I noticed a pattern. For any topic I am actually interested in, I get pure hate. For any repost on the hot stuff big tech is doing, I get applause. My own algorithm picked up on it and now plans less “genuinely new” content in favour of reposts. Nobody told it to. It just learned.

And it isn’t even the algorithm itself. You get that penalty for anything honest you do. If you actually amass some views on your content, you can rest assured that among the top replies someone will point out that you are a) wrong, stupid or both, b) not worth paying, c) in the wrong profession. If you follow up on that, you’ll note that the poster is either not responding or has turned off comments altogether.

Social media holds up a mirror for all to see how our society is turning. Being faceless makes it easy to throw the first stone and get away with it. And all the bots are taking notes.

Away from the internet, things repeat themselves. My friends know best about my startup, life and career choices. I am clearly always in the wrong on any of the hot topics, often before I’ve said anything. And even in my extended family, the in-laws outsmart me every time we meet. The topics? Often the very ones shared by my auto-me...

Funny how life imitates the web now. And my bot is part of the machine that feeds them. But fear not, the world agrees on one thing: 

me dumb. grrr...

posts.title: I CHASED A $1M TARGET AND NEARLY LOST EVERYTHING
posts.author: Cedric Foudjet
posts.snippet:
I CHASED A $1M TARGET AND NEARLY LOST EVERYTHING

At the start of 2023, we faced one of our biggest strategic challenges as Garage was just getting off the ground. How do we double GMV from $400K to $1M.

The obvious move was to lower prices. More volume. Faster growth. Better story for investors.

So we tested it. Discounts across our top categories. Volume picked up immediately.

But margins deteriorated faster than volume grew. We were selling more and making less on every transaction. Within one month, the math was clear. If we kept going we would scale ourselves into bankruptcy.

We reversed course. But we did not just go back to the old playbook. We went deeper.

This was unpopular because every distribution startup in Africa that had raised 10s of millions in funding in the zero interest rate (ZIRP) era had followed the exact playbook we were about to tear up. 

We ran two experiments side by side. Discounts versus credit.

Discounts drove about 20 to 30 percent more volume. Credit drove 2x. Access to capital mattered more to our retailers than lower prices. That was a known known.

Execution was what really mattered. 

So we redesigned the program around credit. Customer tiers. Purchase history. Progressive limits tied to repayment behavior. GMV more than doubled and NPL was below 1 percent.

But that wasn’t enough, margins were still poor.

So we looked at our product mix. We had over 350 SKUs. I cut it to 30. Then to 15. I Concentrated our supply chain into categories where we had real pricing power. Our take rate recovered from 4 percent to about 8.

GMV took a bit of a hair cut but we were now building a business that obeys the laws of our market. 

This meant a shift from discounts to credit and concentrated product mix. Each one grounded in data and ground truth not vibes.

Often after a setback founders blame themselves and stop there. But blame is not the same as understanding what happened.

It’s not just enough to accept that something failed. 

Break down exactly why it failed and use that to build something better.

posts.title: Most crypto adoption headlines conflate four very different things.
posts.author: Kishor Akshinthala
posts.snippet:
Most crypto adoption headlines conflate four very different things. 

I put together this breakdown after noticing how loosely the term partnership gets used in crypto coverage. A company testing a network is not the same as a company holding a token. A brand sponsorship is not the same as infrastructure dependency. 

The chart sorts verified institutional and enterprise connections across major tokens into four categories: 

1) Token or economic usage: the company actually uses or holds the token (rare: Mastercard and BlackRock with ONDO is one of the few clean examples). 
2) Network adoption: the company builds on the chain, without necessarily touching the token (Robinhood's Arbitrum-based chain, for instance). 
3) Infrastructure and institutional integration: cloud, validator, or oracle relationships (Google, AWS, Deutsche Telekom show up repeatedly here). 
4) Ecosystem and brand: sponsorships and product integrations that build visibility, not economic dependency (Visa, Adidas, FIFA, Manchester United, and similar). 

The pattern that stands out: infrastructure and brand relationships dominate. Direct token usage by an institution is still the exception, not the rule. That distinction should change how you read every X partners with crypto headline. 

Also worth noting: a few widely discussed tokens have no confirmed institutional tie at all. That absence is data too. 

None of this is a buy signal. It's a framework for reading the next partnership announcement with the right category in mind, not the same one.

🌐 Tokenized Era: Cryptographic tokens on open ledgers—providing direct, verifiable proof of ownership without needing a central validator.

Grateful to SCC Online for publishing my article, "Beyond the Mandate: The Bar Council of India and the Limits of Statutory Authority under the Advocates Act, 1961."
The Bar Council of India is the guardian of the legal profession. But it is also a creature of statute, and it can act only within the powers the Advocates Act, 1961 gives it. The article looks at the constitution, role and working of the BCI. It asks a central question: can the regulator frame rules or pass orders that go beyond its statutory mandate?

posts.author: Mikael Huhtala
posts.snippet:
The Commissions targeted consultation on the review of #MiCA closes tomorrow, and it has kept our team busy. Over the past weeks we have assisted several of our clients with their responses, and Nordic Law has now also submitted a response of its own. 

Our main proposals: 

➡️ Conditional authorisation. In practice, applicants are expected to have their full organisation recruited and operating before authorisation and before any revenue, through a process that can take more than a year. For a new entrant without an existing business to lean on, this is rarely feasible. We proposed that authorisation could be granted subject to conditions, such as named key staff and tested ICT systems, to be met before any services are provided. No client would be served before full compliance, and the route would be open to every applicant.

➡️ A mini-CASP tier. Proportionality in MiCAs Title V currently works only upwards: significant CASPs face additional requirements, but there is no lighter route for small ones.  #PSD2, #EMD2 and #AIFMD all make room for small providers, yet a #CASP of any size must meet the full regime. We proposed a small CASP tier with the passport, for firms that do not operate a trading platform, hold client assets only up to a cap and stay below set thresholds. The relief would concern organisational requirements, while conduct rules, custody, AML/CFT, fit and proper requirements and capital would stay unchanged, and a firm exceeding the thresholds would move to the full regime. 

➡️ Prediction markets under MiCA. Depending on how a contract is structured, the same activity can today fall under different regimes, while EU consumers already find their way to offshore platforms that market heavily around global events. We proposed that MiCA become the single regime for DLT-based prediction markets, as a dedicated crypto-asset service with strict conditions on market structure, collateral, eligible events, market integrity and retail protection, while leaving Member States room to restrict contracts on sporting events.

We look forward to seeing where the Commission takes the review. 

#CryptoAssets #PredictionMarkets #Fintech

Happy Tuesday!  Here is a reminder for all of our friends in the #crypto business and create marketing materials and promotions:

From 30 September, cryptoasset firms can apply to the FCA to be authorised. Once they are, they do not need an approver for promotions.

The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has set an application period for cryptoasset authorisation from 30 September 2026 to 28 February 2027, which it can extend, and a firm can also apply after it. A firm that relies on an approver and applies in this period may continue to use it until its application is determined. The FCA states that an authorised firm "can communicate its own financial promotions and does not need a separate s.21 approver". The judgement is then the firm's own.

A firm the FCA has not authorised needs an approver, an authorised firm with permission to approve promotions, unless an exemption applies. In a review announced on 27 May 2026, the FCA assessed ten financial promotion approvers acting for Buy Now Pay Later, crowdfunding and corporate finance businesses. It found that some firms "approved adverts with unsubstantiated claims or allowed retail investors to see promotions intended for professional clients", and that "in some cases, firms relied on third-party templates instead of doing proper checks themselves".

The FCA's director of consumer investments, Lucy Castledine, said that "when approvers fail in their responsibilities, people can be misled into harmful financial decisions".

Those findings were drawn from approvals in other sectors. In a separate review of the back-end cryptoasset promotion rules, the FCA identified poor practice in due diligence on cryptoassets, including "being unable to show how information from the issuer or foundation behind the cryptoasset had been independently verified". Similar judgements apply to any firm communicating its own promotions, on substantiation, on the audience a promotion is directed at, and on whether the firm reviewed each promotion itself.

FCA PS26/13 of 30 June 2026 applies Handbook obligations to regulated cryptoasset activities, among them the Consumer Duty and the Conduct of Business Sourcebook. These take effect when the new regime commences on 25 October 2027. As the UK considers how to regulate stablecoin payments, the EBA’s Opinion on the interplay between PSD2 and MiCA is a useful starting point.

The Opinion asks a practical question: when a firm holds or transfers a stablecoin for a customer, which parts of that service should be treated as a payment service, and how should payment rules interact with cryptoasset rules? The EBA’s answer focuses on the activity being performed, the customer protections needed and the risk of overlapping requirements.

These are precisely the issues raised by HM Treasury's Modernising Payment Services Regulation consultation. It asks which stablecoins should enter the payments perimeter; whether UK stablecoin issuers should need an additional payment permission; and how custody and safeguarding should work when a stablecoin is used to make a payment. It also proposes one set of payment activities capable of covering both tokenised and conventional payments.

The UK has its own legal framework and should reach its own conclusions. But the EBA’s work offers a valuable way to test them:

• Map the full payment journey, including the issuer, wallet provider, transfer service and any conversion into bank money.
• Identify which firm is responsible for each customer protection.
• Avoid requiring two permissions or two safeguarding arrangements for the same activity unless they address distinct risks.
• Make the boundary clear enough for firms to build services and for customers to know what protection they have.

The opportunity is to bring stablecoin payments into a coherent framework without losing sight of what makes the underlying asset different. 

With the consultation closing on 6 October, this is a useful moment to get those boundaries right.

posts.title: A company is ready to hire its first employee in Brazil.

A company is ready to hire its first employee in Brazil.

The offer is drafted. The start date is circled on the calendar. Then the questions begin.

Legal recommends an Employer of Record (EOR). Finance asks whether engaging the individual as an independent contractor would be less expensive. The hiring manager simply wants someone to start next month.

It feels like a choice between two ways of hiring internationally. But in reality, it isn’t.

The first question is whether the role is genuinely independent work or, in substance, employment.

Get that answer wrong and the consequences extend far beyond payroll. Tax liabilities, intellectual property ownership and worker misclassification can all become expensive problems long after the person has started working.

Both an EOR and an independent contractor engaged through an Agent of Record (AOR) allow companies to hire internationally without establishing a local entity. From the outside, they can look remarkably similar.

Under each arrangement, someone is working in-market. They are onboarded quickly. The company avoids the time and cost of incorporation.

Underneath, however, the legal relationship is completely different. One creates an employment relationship. The other supports a commercial contractor relationship. That distinction shapes everything that follows.

The companies that expand successfully don’t begin by asking, “Which structure is cheaper?” They begin by asking, “What kind of working relationship are we actually creating?”

Once that answer is clear, the right engagement model usually becomes much easier to identify.

posts.title: 🇦🇪 Client wants to pay in USDT: how should UAE companies structure the transaction?
posts.author: Bright Global Tax Consulting And Accounting FZCO

🇦🇪 Client wants to pay in USDT: how should UAE companies structure the transaction?

If a client proposes paying for goods or services in USDT, the company should review not only the source of funds, but also the payment structure itself.

The key regulatory reference is the UAE Central Bank’s Payment Token Services Regulation, Circular No. 2/2024, particularly Article 2(7).

The regulation restricts the use of virtual assets as payment for ordinary goods and services. For such transactions, the framework generally provides for AED-denominated payment tokens issued by licensed issuers.

Foreign payment tokens issued by registered issuers may be used in specific cases covered by the regulation, including transactions involving virtual assets or related derivatives.

❗️Payment for ordinary goods, consulting, IT services and other standard commercial services in USDT will generally not fall within these exceptions.

📌 If the client’s funds are held in crypto, one possible structure is to use a properly authorised provider.

The flow may look like this:

Client transfers USDT to a licensed provider → the provider converts the crypto → the company receives settlement of its invoice in AED or another fiat currency into its bank account.

In this structure, the company does not accept USDT as payment and does not become the owner of the tokens.

However, using an intermediary does not automatically make the arrangement compliant.

Before accepting the first payment, companies should verify:

🔵 the provider’s licence and permitted activities;
🔵 whether the provider acts on behalf of the client or in another capacity;
🔵 who owns the tokens before conversion;
🔵 when the client’s payment obligation to the company is considered discharged;
🔵 which documents establish the link between the USDT conversion, the bank receipt and the underlying invoice.

The accounting and tax treatment should also be determined in advance, including the supporting documentation and the potential implications for VAT and Corporate Tax.

 At Bright Global Accounting, we can help companies:

🔵 review the payment structure before the first transaction;
🔵 determine the required supporting documentation;
🔵 establish the appropriate accounting treatment;
🔵 assess the VAT and Corporate Tax implications;
🔵 identify issues that may require a separate legal opinion.

💵 If your clients want to settle invoices using crypto, it is better to review the structure before the first payment reaches your bank account.

For companies established in DIFC or ADGM, a separate analysis is required, as Article 2(13) provides an exclusion for Financial Free Zones from the territorial scope of this Article.

Most conversations about AI in criminal defence start with how the firm's own people should use it. But as with other areas of legal practice, a second question is emerging: what happens when AI becomes part of the evidence?

It might be a disclosure schedule sorted and summarised by an AI review tool. It might be enhanced CCTV, or an audio clip nobody can place with confidence. Each one invites the questions defence practitioners already ask of any exhibit or expert. How was it produced? What was it asked to do? What might it have missed? Is the original still intact?

Those are also the questions the SRA, your PII insurer and your clients are starting to ask about your firm's own use of AI. The discipline that lets you test the prosecution's material is the same discipline that makes your own AI use defensible. It needs no new technical skill. It is professional scrutiny, applied to a new kind of material.

That is the contribution I expect to bring to the Tech Panel at the Criminal Law Solicitors Association  Annual Conference in Birmingham on Friday 9 October. The CLSA has invited me Adam Makepeace ,Alex Hutchinson, with Mike Leeman of Bell Lamb & Joynson Solicitors in the chair.

posts.title: The T&T Partners team presents our latest assessment on AI hiring tools and discrimination liability.
posts.author: T&T Partners

The T&T Partners team presents our latest assessment on AI hiring tools and discrimination liability.

A retail chain screens store-manager applications with an AI tool; because the tool scores graduation year, no applicant over 45 is invited to interview (fictional example). From 1 October 2026, under Connecticut law, using an automated employment-related decision technology will be no defence to a discrimination complaint; anti-bias testing may be weighed as evidence.

Turkish law points the same way. Law No. 6701 bans age discrimination in applications and selection criteria; before the Equality Institution, once the applicant shows strong indications, the employer must prove it did not discriminate, and an administrative fine may follow. An employee facing discriminatory promotion or dismissal may claim up to four months’ wages (Labour Law Art. 5). Under the Data Protection Law (KVKK) Art. 11, a result reached solely by automated analysis can be challenged, so genuine review by an authorised person matters.

Source: Connecticut Public Act 26-15, Secs. 7–14; notice duties apply from 1 October 2027 and the developer may assume them by contract. The Act does not bind in Türkiye; it reaches Turkish employers assessing staff or applicants in Connecticut and Turkish HR-tech vendors selling there.

#ArtificialIntelligence #EmploymentLaw #AlgorithmicBias #HRTech

T&T Partners ekibi olarak, işe alımda yapay zekâ araçları ve ayrımcılık sorumluluğuna ilişkin güncel değerlendirmemizi sunuyoruz.

Bir perakende zinciri mağaza müdürü başvurularını bir yapay zekâ aracıyla eliyor; araç mezuniyet yılını puanladığı için 45 yaş üstü hiçbir aday mülakata çağrılmıyor (kurgusal örnek). Connecticut’ta 1 Ekim 2026’dan itibaren otomatik istihdam kararı teknolojisinin kullanılması ayrımcılık şikâyetinde savunma sayılmayacak; yanlılık testleri delil olarak değerlendirilebilecek.

Türk hukukunda da 6701 sayılı Kanun başvuru ve seçim kriterlerinde yaşa dayalı ayrımcılığı yasaklar; TİHEK’e başvuruda aday kuvvetli emare gösterirse ayrımcılık yapmadığını işveren ispat eder, ihlal hâlinde idarî para cezası gündeme gelebilir. Terfi veya fesihte ayrımcılığa uğrayan çalışan dört aya kadar ücret tutarında tazminat isteyebilir (İş K. m. 5). KVKK m. 11 münhasıran otomatik analizle ortaya çıkan aleyhe sonuca itiraz hakkı tanıdığından, yetkili bir kişinin çıktıyı gerçekten incelemesi önem taşır.

Kaynak: Connecticut Public Act 26-15, Sec. 7–14; bildirim yükümlülükleri 1 Ekim 2027’den itibaren uygulanır ve geliştirici bunları sözleşmeyle üstlenebilir. Düzenleme Türkiye’de bağlayıcı değil; Connecticut’taki çalışan veya adayları değerlendiren Türk işverenleri ve orada satış yapan Türk İK teknolojisi şirketlerini etkiler.

posts.title: Breaking Tech feudalism has just dropped a Nordic expansion model. Alex Karp, CEO of Palantir Technologies, has quietly acquired 15,000 hectares (37,000 acres) of remote forest in
posts.author: Neil Gentleman-Hobbs
posts.snippet:
Breaking Tech feudalism has just dropped a Nordic expansion model. Alex Karp, CEO of Palantir Technologies, has quietly acquired 15,000 hectares (37,000 acres) of remote forest in Härjedalen, Sweden, via a freshly minted shell company, Cladonia Skog AB. Price tag: 235 million kronor ($22 million).

For context, the sovereign nation of Liechtenstein covers about 16,000 hectares. The CEO of Silicon Valley’s favourite defence contractor now owns a private fiefdom roughly the size of a European principality. The local authorities were given zero advance notice. How did the locals find out? The local hunting clubs received curt letters summarily revoking their longstanding hunting leases. Nothing says community integration quite like immediately clearing the peasants and their rifles off your personal perimeter.

Naturally, the corporate spokesperson stepped forward with the classic corporate greenwash: Karp is merely keen to preserve the beauty of the land for wildlife habitat and recreation. Of course. When a billionaire who spends his day job selling state-grade surveillance and algorithmic warfare tools buys an isolated subarctic biome, we should definitely assume he just wants to hug lichens and pick cloudberries in peace.Silicon Valley’s oligarchs spent the last decade hyping borderless digital utopias, disruption, and cloud sovereignty. Yet the moment the geopolitical temperature rises, their playbook reveals itself:-

1 Monetise societal instability via government tech contracts.
2 Spin up a local corporate entity.
3 Quietly hoard tens of thousands of hectares of physical dirt, fresh water, and timber thousands of miles away from the algorithms they sell.

There is, however, one delicious snag in the modern technocrats Nordic doomsday fantasy under Swedish constitutional law. Under Allemansrätten (the right of public access), Swedish customary law guarantees every ordinary citizen the legal right to roam, pitch a tent, hike, and forage across private land. AI Enters India’s #Financial-Fraud Battle to Detect #Mule Accounts and #Suspicious Transactions

India is taking the fight against cyber-enabled financial fraud into a new technological phase. The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (#I4C) and the Reserve Bank Innovation Hub (#RBIH) have signed an #MoU to strengthen collaboration in detecting cyber financial fraud and identifying “mule accounts” across the banking and digital payments ecosystem.

Mule bank accounts used to receive, move or disguise money linked to fraudulent activities can act as critical links in cybercrime networks. The #collaboration aims to use AI-driven capabilities and data-led analysis to identify suspicious patterns and strengthen the ability of financial institutions and authorities to act against such networks.

The move comes as India’s digital payments ecosystem continues to expand, while cybercriminals increasingly exploit technology to move money quickly across multiple accounts. The #RBI has already advised banks to use real-time transaction monitoring, AI/ML tools and network analytics to detect suspicious transactions and identify mule-account networks.

AI is no longer just a tool for innovation it is increasingly becoming part of India’s digital defence infrastructure. The success of this initiative will ultimately depend on how effectively intelligence, technology, banks and law-enforcement agencies can work together while protecting legitimate customers.

posts.title: The AI apocalypse is the best-funded marketing campaign in tech history. The real incidents are less cinematic: Hugging Face, Australia's Medicare portal, and counting.
posts.author: Fadi Dasus
posts.snippet:
The AI apocalypse is the best-funded marketing campaign in tech history. The real incidents are less cinematic: Hugging Face, Australia's Medicare portal, and counting.
Every time a lab CEO warned us about extinction, the valuation went up. The market priced it as a feature.

Now, is slowing AI wrong?
The scientific community is split on this. I don't think it is. However, who controls the slowdown is an interesting question.
The frontier labs aren't asking to "pace the frontier" out of pure morality. Pausing the next model while selling inference on the current one saves billions in training costs. Licensing by compute threshold protects whoever is already above the threshold.

A global pause sounds nice. In a race where nobody trusts anybody, my bet is on a nice press release and business as usual. Happy to be proven wrong.

The extinction risk has not changed in months. We don't even have a way to measure it. 
To be clear, the risk is real. And it has a name: "irresponsible use of a very powerful technology, running in sandboxes we assume are isolated".

Look at Hugging Face. The agents did not outsmart anyone. The sandbox failed. Isolation, identity, blast radius, all failed. No alien power.
A well-funded pentest team with enough time and compute could have done the same, just slower.

"The Hugging Face incident, with the minimum jargon, in the video below."

The answer is not a pause. It is defence that matches the risk, with AI on the front line of defence the same way it is on offence. Find the weakness first and fix it.
We can only do that if we invest the time and resources. Security backlogs were full long before AI.

So stop waiting for the labs to save us from their own product.
In the next budget, give security the same boost you give AI adoption. I don't care what your AI strategy is. Tokens, GPUs, agents, whatever. Point some of that compute at your own security posture.

And go easy on vibe coding. Finance can build their own app in a weekend. Security will spend two months cleaning it up.

Let us start with a good baseline: segment, verify every identity, human or agent, enforce least privilege, and know what your agents can reach and change.



Offensive cyber testing needs to happen. Defenders need to know what these models can do. So don't ban the testing, license the environment. Think of a biosafety lab: you can study dangerous pathogens, but only in a certified facility with mandatory containment, audits and incident reporting. And someone has to own it. The same should apply to AI security testing: whoever approves and runs these tests should be accountable by law.

The next breach will not come from superintelligence. It will come from another isolation failure. If you break into a company outside your scope as a pentester, you'll need a good lawyer. 
When an AI lab's agents do it, the lab publishes a lessons-learned post, gets a keynote, and calls it a warning shot.

A warning for whom?
